meta.title: Who really said "An aim in life is the only fortune worth finding"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote it in The Amateur Emigrant, ch. 4. Napoleon Hill popularised it in 1928, crediting Stevenson.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'An aim in life is the only fortune worth finding'?
meta.ogDescription: Stevenson, not Onassis. The line is from The Amateur Emigrant (ch. 4, Steerage Types); Napoleon Hill reprinted it in 1928, crediting Stevenson.

answer.label: Robert Louis Stevenson — popularised by Napoleon Hill
answer.authorDates: 1850–1894 · Scottish novelist, essayist and travel writer
answer.sourceLine: Stevenson wrote it in The Amateur Emigrant, his account of the 1879 emigrant crossing to New York — chapter 4, “Steerage Types ↗” — where the sentence runs “an aim in life is the only fortune worth the finding.” Napoleon Hill reprinted the line as a display epigraph in The Law of Success (1928) and credited Stevenson underneath it ↗; the trimmed wording that circulates today is his setting, and the credit fell off along the way.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Part I, “From the Clyde to Sandy Hook” — ch. 4, “Steerage Types”
Written 1879–80; first published in full in 1895
Napoleon Hill, The Law of Success (1928) — a display epigraph, credited to Stevenson

source.excerpt: You cannot run away from a weakness; you must some time fight it out or perish; and if that be so, why not now, and where you stand? … A sea-voyage will not give a man the nerve to put aside cheap pleasure; emigration has to be done before we climb the vessel; an aim in life is the only fortune worth the finding; and it is not to be found in foreign lands, but in the heart itself.
trail: The primary text. The sentence appears verbatim in ch. 4, “Steerage Types,” of The Amateur Emigrant: “emigration has to be done before we climb the vessel; an aim in life is the only fortune worth the finding; and it is not to be found in foreign lands, but in the heart itself.” Confirmed in Wikisource’s transcription of the 1911 Charles Scribner’s Sons Biographical Edition ↗ (the book itself was first published in full in 1895).

A second independent text. The same paragraph, word for word, in Project Gutenberg’s edition of The Works of Robert Louis Stevenson, Swanston Edition, vol. 2 (Chatto and Windus, 1911) ↗, under the “Steerage Types” heading — an independent London printing rather than a different era: both witnesses cited here are 1911 reprints, from different publishers on opposite sides of the Atlantic.

Where Hill comes in. The scan of the 1928 Ralston University Press printing of The Law of Success shows the line set as a display page closing the Introductory Lesson, in capitals, signed “—Robert Louis Stevenson” — and with the dropped before “finding.” Internet Archive full text ↗.

Publication history. Stevenson wrote the book in 1879–80 after sailing for California; it was not published in full until 1895, one year after his death, per Wikipedia’s article on the work ↗. The quotation-research site WIST ↗ cites it the same way: The Amateur Emigrant, ch. 4 “Steerage Types” (1895).
source.excerptNote: Note the word the popular version loses: Stevenson wrote “worth the finding.” The shorter form now in circulation is the one Hill set in 1928.

author.name: Robert Louis Stevenson
author.heading: Who wrote it
author.metaLine: 1850–1894 · Scottish novelist, essayist, travel writer and poet
author.bio: Stevenson was a Scottish novelist, essayist, travel writer and poet, best known for Treasure Island, Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, Kidnapped and A Child’s Garden of Verses. In August 1879 he sailed for California to reunite with Fanny Osbourne, travelling second class on the steamship Devonia and then overland by train — a journey that nearly broke his health and produced The Amateur Emigrant. He died in 1894, and the book appeared in full the following year.

misattribution.heading: How the credit went wrong
misattribution.intro: The words and the trim do trace to one page of one 1928 self-help book — but that page credits Stevenson, correctly and in print. The wrong name arrived later, downstream, once harvesters had lifted the display page without its credit line.

items.why: Wikiquote lists the line in the “Misattributed” section of its Onassis page ↗ and names the vector: “Attributed in Wisdom Through the Ages: Book Two (2003) by Helen Granat, p. 118.” Granat’s anthology is where the wrong name enters. A quotation aggregator mirrors the Onassis filing ↗, correct citation to Stevenson and all.

Hill set the sentence as a display page closing the Introductory Lesson of The Law of Success (1928), in capitals, and signed it “—Robert Louis Stevenson” directly underneath. The scan of that printing ↗ shows the credit line plainly. Hill never claimed it, and nobody credits him as its author; harvesters took the words off his page and left the attribution behind.

The 1928 epigraph drops the article, and that shorter form is the one in circulation. Stevenson’s own text keeps it: “an aim in life is the only fortune worth the finding” — see the chapter on Wikisource ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Stevenson’s, from The Amateur Emigrant, ch. 4 “Steerage Types” — verifiable in the chapter text ↗ and in Project Gutenberg’s Swanston Edition, vol. 2 (1911) ↗.

context.heading: Why it landed
lead: It reads like a motivational poster, which is roughly what Hill turned it into. In its own setting it is something sharper: hard-eyed reporting from the steerage deck. Stevenson had sailed from the Clyde in 1879 among emigrants he was actually living beside, and he came away unconvinced by the promise the voyage was selling. Drink, idleness and incompetency, he wrote, were the three great causes of emigration — and a boat fixes none of them.

So the sentence is an argument, not an aspiration. “Emigration has to be done before we climb the vessel” — change your country and you change only the scenery; the aim has to be found first, and it is found inward. That is why the word “fortune” bites: these were people crossing an ocean to look for money, and Stevenson is telling them the only fortune that travels is the one they would have to bring.
context.detailsSummary: Why the book took until 1895 to appear
detailsBody: Stevenson wrote The Amateur Emigrant in 1879–80, but it was not published in full until 1895, one year after his death. Part I was ready for the press and then withdrawn in 1880 ↗.

His circle disliked it: his close association with working-class passengers offended middle-class sensibilities, certain passages struck the publisher as too graphic, and his father Thomas Stevenson bought all the copies of the already printed travelogue, judging it beneath his son’s talent — per Wikipedia’s account ↗. The line that later became inspirational boilerplate was, in its own moment, part of a book his family tried to bury.
